utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I call the Registrar -- to ask the Registrar to call out the number and name of this case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is IT-95-17/1-I, the Prosecutor against Anto Furundzija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me check whether the equipment for interpretation works. I would like to ask the accused if he can hear me in a language he understands. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We may now commence with this hearing. As you know, this is the initial appearance of the accused before the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. This hearing is being held in accordance with the Statute of the Tribunal and our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, to charge formally the accused. As you know, these proceedings are being recorded and will be available to the public. Rule 62 of the Rules of Procedure requires that the accused, after having his indictment confirmed by a judge and after having been arrested and surrendered to the custody of the International Tribunal, must be formally charged at a procedure described as the initial appearance. I would like now to ask the accused to rise and state for the Trial Chamber his name, date and place of birth and the name of the attorney whom he has chosen to represent him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: My name is Anto Furundzija, born 8th July 1969, in Travnik, in Travnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I have the name of your attorney, the attorney you have chosen?

utterances.speaker: MR. FURUNDZIJA
utterances.text: Mr Joka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FURUNDZIJA
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I have the appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr President, your Honours and counsel. My name is Mark Harmon, I represent the Prosecutor's Office this afternoon in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now turn to the counsel for the accused and I would like to ask him to introduce himself. Could you introduce yourself and spell your name clearly? Please would you also indicate which bar you work with.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Srdjan Joka, I am an attorney from Croatia and am a member of the Bar Association of the Republic of Croatia. I was told to spell my name, S-R-D-J-A-N J-O-K-A. I think that is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could you confirm that your qualifications, credentials and other necessary documents have been provided to the Registry of our Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that, and I can add that I am on a register of the appointed Defence counsel at the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me say a few words about the rules which govern our proceedings today, and I will try simply to summarise them very quickly. As you know, Article 20 of the Statute of the International Criminal Tribunal requires us inter alia first of all to satisfy ourselves that the rights of the accused are respected; then to confirm that the accused understands the indictment, and thirdly, call upon the accused to enter a plea to the charges against him in the indictment. You may also know that the rights of the accused are detailed in Article 21 of the Tribunal's Statute. This article provides inter alia that the accused shall be entitled to a fair and public hearing, he shall be informed promptly and in detail, in a language which he understands, of the nature and cause of the charges against him, and that he must be given adequate time and facilities for the preparation of his defence and to communicate with counsel of his own choosing. As I have already indicated, Rule 62 of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal governs the initial appearance. This Trial Chamber must be satisfied that the accused's right to counsel has been respected, the indictment must be read to the accused in a language he speaks or understands and the Trial Chamber must be satisfied that the accused understands the indictment. We are then required to call upon the accused to enter a plea of guilty or not guilty on each count. If the accused fails to enter a plea, we are required to enter a plea of not guilty on his behalf. In the case of a not guilty plea, we will instruct the Registrar to set a date for trial. In the case of a guilty plea, we will instruct the Registrar to set a date for the pre-sentencing hearing, or any other appropriate dates. Now I would like to ask Defence counsel whether he and his client have received copies of the indictment in a language which they understand and whether the contents therein were understood. Have you had adequate time to confer with your client in preparation for this initial appearance? This is a question addressed to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Your Honours, both my client and I have received the indictment and had adequate time to prepare for this initial appearance before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Now the indictment, as you know, was issued by the Prosecutor on 2nd November 1995, and it was confirmed by Judge Gabrielle Kirk McDonald on 10th November 1995. Judge McDonald also ordered that the indictment should not be divulged. This order still applies and the reading of the indictment today will be in compliance here with. So in principle under our Statute and our Rules, as I say, the indictment should be read out here in court. I wonder, however, whether the accused is prepared to waive his right to the public reading of the indictment. I wonder whether he has been in touch with the Defence counsel on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours, we have discussed this subject and my client -- he has a very clear idea what it concerns and on our part, we agree that there is no need to read it here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now turn to the accused. May I ask you please to rise, Mr Furundzija? Thank you. Your counsel has informed the Trial Chamber that you have received a copy of the indictment in a language which you understand, that you comprehend the contents of the indictment. The indictment has just been read -- you waived your right to the public reading out of the indictment. I would like to ask you whether you may confirm whether this is correct, whether the indictment is correct, whatever I have been saying is correct and whether you have any questions concerning the indictment. This is my main question, whether you have any questions concerning the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FURUNDZIJA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no questions and it is correct what my counsel has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I am now going to recall each of the three counts against you. Please tell the court whether you plead guilty or not guilty after I have put the counts to you, each of the three counts to you. The form of words we wish you to use is, "I plead guilty", or, "I plead not guilty". Have you understood that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FURUNDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I will ask you about count 12, a grave breach, torture or inhuman treatment recognised by Article 2(b) of the Tribunal's Statute. How do you plead?

utterances.speaker: MR. FURUNDZIJA
utterances.text: I plead not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Count 13, a violation of the laws or customs of war, torture, recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal's Statute; how do you plead?

utterances.speaker: MR. FURUNDZIJA
utterances.text: I plead not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Count 14, a violation of the laws or customs of war, outrages upon personal dignity, including rape, recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal's Statute; how do you plead?

utterances.speaker: MR. FURUNDZIJA
utterances.text: I plead not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may now be seated. Mr Furundzija, you will be remanded now to the further custody of the International Tribunal, and kept in the detention unit until further order is made. Would the Registrar please note the pleas of the accused? As the accused has pleaded not guilty to the charges against him, it is necessary to consider the organisation of the work of the Trial Chamber and the setting of a date for the trial. May I ask the Registrar whether the Registry is able to set a date for the trial right away?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I cannot answer this question at this moment, but the Registry will do everything it can to set the date for the trial as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We shall therefore have to await confirmation from the Registry. Let me now move on to a few problems which I would like to -- questions which I would like to raise. First of all, let me remind briefly the obligations of the Prosecutor. Under our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Prosecutor has an obligation, and this is spelt out in Rule 66, to make available to the Defence within 30 days of this initial appearance copies of the supporting material which accompanied the indictment when confirmation was sought, and all prior statements obtained by the Office of the Prosecutor from the accused. This is a clear obligation set out in our Rules. Furthermore, the Prosecutor is obliged to make available, no later than 60 days before the date set for trial, copies of the statements of all witnesses whom the Prosecutor intends to call to testify at trial. The statements of any additional witnesses shall be made available as soon as decisions to call those witnesses are made. Further orders may be made by the Trial Chamber in the interests of a fair and expeditious trial for the accused. I would like to ask if any such documents have already been provided to the Defence; if not, may I ask the Prosecutor if he could indicate a timeframe within which these materials can be provided to Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr President, no such materials have been provided to the Defence to date. We will comply with the Rules set forth in Rule 66, we will provide all supporting materials to the Defence within 30 days of the initial appearance. My best estimate at this point, Mr President, is that we will provide these supporting materials to counsel on or before 5th January, which is well within the timeframe set up in Rule 66. I am not in a position to comment on the second part of the Rule, that is when we have to provide the statements of all witnesses, but we will comply with the Rule, that is we will comply with providing the statements within 60 days, no later than 60 days before the date set for trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr Joka, do you understand what the Prosecutor has just pledged? So you will be entitled within the timeframe he has just set out to have all the documents that were attached to the indictment and the request for confirmation which were submitted to the International Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have completely understood that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: I only wanted to ask my learned colleague that if possible, and observing the timeframe from Rule 66, if he could provide these documents as soon as possible, but I think that we will meet that deadline anyway. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. I see that you are nodding, so you agree. Let me also address the issue of preliminary motions. You know that Rule 72 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence provide for preliminary motions. The parties under this particular Rule of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence have 60 days from the date of disclosure by the Prosecutor to the Defence of all material and statements provided under Rule 66(A), within which they must file preliminary motions, if any. Other motions may be filed under Rule 73. I wonder whether the parties might indicate their general readiness to proceed to trial. First of all, let me turn to the Defence counsel. Generally speaking, are you ready to proceed to trial as soon as these questions are sorted out?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Of course it is in our interest to have as early a date for trial as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr President, after the hearing and decisions rendered on the preliminary motions, we will be ready to proceed to trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much. One final point which is of relevance to us concerning the organisation of the proceedings is the question of the Status Conference, which as you know is of great importance. So we should be able to set a date for a Status Conference in order to look in greater detail at the state of preparedness of the parties for trial, and also in order to settle any outstanding issues. I wonder whether the Prosecutor could suggest a suitable date for a Status Conference. Are you in a position to propose a date?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am not at this point, Mr President. I have not seen any -- the complexity of any preliminary motions. I think it would be, first of all, of interest to us to see the preliminary motions, what they are, before we can set a Status Conference date. If the court wishes a date set before the filing of the preliminary motions, then, Mr President, we are at the court's disposal. I would say -- I do not have a calendar in front of me, I would suggest perhaps toward the end of January, a date for a Status Conference. By then we will have complied with our initial discovery obligations under Rule 66, counsel will have had an opportunity to see the supporting materials and at that point, perhaps a Status Conference would be in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder whether the Defence counsel has any suggestion concerning a Status Conference, a date for a Status Conference?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will cooperate as much as possible within the timeframe that we are operating in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We judges were thinking that two dates might be suitable; one would be 13th February in the afternoon, or the other one would be, if this is not acceptable to the parties, would be 16th March at 8.30 in the morning. Of course, we would prefer 13th February, the sooner the better.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Either date is convenient to the Prosecutor, Mr President. Either date, it does not make any difference to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: What about the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: We are prepared to comply with the first or the second date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So therefore let us go for 13th February in the afternoon, probably 2.30 or 3.00 in the afternoon, 13th February, for a Status Conference. All right, it is so decided. Now I would like to ask the parties to notify to the Trial Chamber, through the Registry, of course, of any problems that may arise in the meantime, in order that we may dispose of those problems and proceed with a fair and expeditious trial, because we very much believe, and we have strong feelings about that, that the accused has a fundamental right to a fair and expeditious trial. I wonder whether there are any questions that either party might wish to raise? Yes, please. Any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Not within this context, your Honours. Maybe just for me for my own clarifications' sake, I am here for the first time, I did not fully understand your initial remarks. Was this indictment now public, the indictment pursuant to Rule 53, or whether this indictment continues to be under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It is public, there was an order issued yesterday, I think, to the effect that the indictment is public, in part, of course, because some parts are redacted, so the part of the indictment concerning your client is public. Any other questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: No, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. And from the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No additional questions, Mr President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder whether my colleagues would like to raise any questions? No questions? All right, so therefore the hearing may be adjourned. The hearing is adjourned.
